With less than 4 years remaining until their deadline, until only 35% of the SDGs targets are on track. Delivering on the SDGs in this last mile demands collective resolve. It also requires coherent policy guidance by governments. And improved coordination and collaboration across all the United Nations system. And it begins here, with the ECOSOC system, which brings a remarkable wealth of expertise, of evidence, of data and policy insight across the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development. At a time of interconnected crises and rapid change, we must ask how this system— the ECOSOC system— The ECOSOC architecture can operate more effectively and in a more integrated manner to deliver its full potential. The ongoing review process, including the UNAT Initiative, the General Assembly review of ECOSOC, and the HPLF, HLPF, and the OCOSOC's forthcoming 2027 review of its subsidiary body are important opportunities to this end. As we enter the final stretch toward 2030, the challenge is not It is not simply to do more. It is to work better together. To deliver. How do we ensure that the Council's subsidiary architecture functions as a force multiplier for SDG delivery in the final stretch towards 2030? This is the task of the ECOSOC itself. Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. The Commission on Narcotic Drugs, CND, as the United Nations principal policymaking body on drug control with treaty-based functions, continues to see strong engagement and increasing demand on its work. In this context, enhancing effectiveness and responsiveness is essential. Allow me to highlight 3 priority areas alongside concrete recommendations for ECOSOC and its subsidiary bodies. First, actionable outcomes and follow-up. The CND's intersessional thematic discussions grounded in UNODC data and expertise, have proven to be a valuable platform for sharing national experiences, lessons learned, and good practices in implementing international drug policy commitments contained in the 2019 and 2024 Ministerial Declarations. They also promote inclusive participation across governments, international organizations, civil society, and the scientific community. The Pledge for Action spotlights during these thematic discussions provide Member States an opportunity to update the Commission on progress made in the implementation of the commitments they made at the time of the 2024 Ministerial segment. As a matter of recommendation, ECOSOC may wish to better leverage the technical outputs of its subsidiary bodies by ensuring these are systematically reflected in Council policy documents. In addition, the Council and its subsidiary bodies could promote structured follow-up mechanisms, such as strengthened pledge monitoring, to translate commitments into measurable progress. Second, coherence across the system. The CND benefits from collaborating with other functional commissions, including not only the Vienna-based Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, but also the Statistical Commission, the Commission on the Status of Women, and the Commission on Science and Technology for Development. A useful practice is the roundtable which one of my predecessors, the CND Chair of the 67th session, held at the margins of the 2024 ECOSOC Coordination Segment, seeking the views of other functional commissions ahead of the CND's 2024 ministerial segment. Further strengthening system-wide coherence remains critical to addressing the complex, cross-cutting nature of drug-related challenges. The Council may wish to foster stronger horizontal cooperation by increasing the visibility of joint substantive work across its subsidiary bodies. Moreover, enabling Chairs of the functional commissions, particularly those based outside New York, to regularly present their outcomes at ECOSOC would ensure that their expertise is more fully integrated into Council deliberations and decision-making. Third, technological innovation and working methods. Recent experience within the CND has demonstrated that the hybrid meeting format and use of modern technology significantly enhance inclusivity, allowing capital-based experts to participate effectively and cost-efficiently. ECOSOC could take the lead in modernizing intergovernmental working methods by enabling hybrid formats and the use of modern technology in formal proceedings. meetings. Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Excellencies. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Least Developed Countries. The Group welcomes this timely discussion as we enter the final years of implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the Doha Programme of Action. Mr. Vice President, for the LDCs, the key question is not whether we reform institutions, but whether those reforms result in stronger support for most vulnerable countries facing the greatest structural challenges. As discussions on UNAID and the review of ECOSOC's subsidiary architecture advance, we must ensure that efficiency gains translate into greater development impact on the ground. On the first question regarding how ECOSOC subsidiary bodies can better translate analysis into action, the LDC Group believes that recommendations must be accompanied by clear implementation pathways, sustained financing, accountability mechanisms, and follow-up arrangements. Too often, valuable analytical work does not sufficiently influence operational activities and financing decisions. We therefore call for a stronger transmission of recommendations from ECOSOC subsidiary bodies into country-level implementation through the Resident Coordinator System and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. Aligned with national development priorities and context. Systematic tracking of implementation of key recommendations affecting LDCs, including those related to financing, climate resilience, productive capacity development, and sustainable graduation support. Greater use of evidence from countries in special situations to inform ECOSOC deliberations and policy guidance. On the second question, concerning coherence and reducing duplication across subsidiary architecture, the LDC Group underscores that UN development system must be strengthened, diversity of the mandates be respected, and system-wide coordination be enhanced. However, efficiency should not come at the expense of political attention to the unique needs of the LDCs. We thus stress better alignment of the work of ECOSOC subsidiary bodies with the 6 priority areas of Doha Programme of Action, enhanced coordination among functional commissions, expert bodies and regional commissions on issues that cut across development, finance, climate and resilience; preservation and strengthening of LDC-specific mandates and priorities in the outcome of the UNAID initiative. The review of subsidiary machinery should identify overlaps while also addressing existing gaps in support to countries furthest behind. On the third question regarding integrated approaches, LDCs strongly support a more holistic approach across ECOSOC architecture. From LDC's perspective, development challenges do not occur in silos. Climate vulnerability affects food security and inclusive growth. Debt pressures constrain social investment. Weak productive capacities limit resilience and economic diversification. ECOSOC subsidiary bodies should therefore act as a force multiplier by promoting integrated solutions that connect financing, climate action, trade, technological innovation, productive capacity development, and social protection. We underscore joint and cross-cutting work programs among relevant subsidiary bodies on issues affecting countries in a special situation, more systematic engagement between ECOSOC bodies and the Financing for Development, Climate, and Development Cooperation processes, stronger support for nationally warned integrated strategies that advance both SDG implementation and DPOA priorities. In closing, Mr. Vice President, as we approach the 2027 DPOA review, The group believes that success should be measured by whether ECOSOC's subsidiarity architecture becomes more responsive, more coordinated, and more action-oriented for LDCs facing the greatest development challenges. We view the UNAID initiative as an opportunity to build a more effective and efficient United Nations system. For LDCs, this must mean delivering tangible results, increased ODA and resilience, technology transfer, accelerated SDG progress, strengthen productive capacities, sustainable graduation pathways, and fulfillment of international commitments under Doha Programme of Action. Let us be clear: no reform effort will be successful if it leaves the LDCs still waiting for delivery. I thank you.

UNECE's unique role, with more than 30 environmental conventions, 57 transport agreements, and over 250 global technical regulations and standards, illustrates the value of grounding activities in clear legal obligations or SDG requirements. We also appreciate the efforts of the other regional commissions in implementing changes arising from the UNEP initiative and encourage continued efforts to ensure its successful implementation. Finally, we encouraged all ECOSOC subsidiary bodies to make full use of the guidance developed by the Working Group, including concept notes, templates, as well as review and retirement clauses in support of the effective implementation of Resolution 80/251. These tools are among the most significant UN-AIT deliverables, and their consistent application by the UN system including ECOSOC subsidiary bodies, will be essential to achieving the coherence and focus we collectively seek. And I thank you.
I thank the distinguished Ambassador, Permanent Representative of Poland, and now give the floor to the representative of Indonesia, to be followed by Canada and Algeria.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Indonesia welcomes this timely roundtable and thanks the presenters for their insightful briefings. And for helping frame this timely discussion. As we approach the final mile of the 2030 Agenda, ECOSOC subsidiary architecture has an important role to play in making the work of the Council more coherent, responsive, and results-oriented. For Indonesia, 3 points are essential. First, greater coherence across ECOSOC subsidiary bodies is important. Functional commissions expert bodies, and regional commissions should be encouraged to work in a more connected manner, reduce institutional silos, and provide clearer, more integrated policy messages. Coherence should not remain a procedural objective. It should translate into tangible impact for the people and communities we serve. Their recommendations should be action-oriented, evidence-based, and accessible to policymakers, at the country level, including through stronger use of regional platforms, South-South and triangular cooperation, and national and local expertise. Reform of ECOSOC's working methods should also strengthen inclusivity and trust. Smaller delegations and developing countries must be able to engage meaningfully in the work of subsidiary bodies. Second, ECOSOC strengthening should not unfold in isolation. It takes place alongside the broader UNEP process, and both tracks can be mutually reinforcing. At the same time, any reform effort should remain firmly grounded in intergovernmental mandates and guided by the priorities set by member states. Third, effectiveness requires adequate means of implementation. For many developing countries, the final mile to 2030. depends on financing, technology transfer, capacity building, data systems, and resilient institutions. ECOSOC subsidiary bodies should therefore help identify gaps, mobilize partnerships, and provide integrated guidance that supports the balanced implementation of the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Indonesia and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Canada, to be followed by Algeria, Vice President Sylvain Cassot.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, and thank you to the distinguished delegates for your insightful comments this morning. Before I begin my response, I would like to point back to one of the panelists' remarks, specifically Mr. Alter, who mentioned that countries benefit from the use of common strategic frameworks and principles. goals. I'd like to share that since 2021, the United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management, or UNGGIM, has witnessed over 100 countries using our framework, the United Nations Integrated Geospatial Information Framework, to implement or to advance geospatial infrastructures within their respective countries. This is a significant achievement related to the adoption of a UN framework. This framework is focused on governance, on technology, and people, and it's used to connect knowledge across disciplines, whether that's economic, social, environmental resilience, or focused on revitalization. To the delegate from Mozambique who suggested that perhaps mapping of recommendations be considered. To the delegate from Canada, thank you for your questions specifically related to collaboration between ECOSOC subsidiary bodies. I'd like to point to our working group focused on integrating geospatial and statistical information. This group reports to both the Statistical Commission and the UNGGIM Committee of Experts. Together, we have worked very hard to publish information about how best to use statistical frameworks for success, and we can share more information about that with you. And then finally, are recommendations adequately being tracked? I would say yes. Our working groups, whether those focused on land administration, geodesy, Integrating geospatial and statistical data, marine geospatial data. The working groups are very active, and every year the expectation is such that when you come to the annual meeting in August, you'll have a full report on how you advanced since the last session. The working groups are ensuring this throughout the year with regular meetings. I will say this can be further demonstrated that we've recently opened 2 centers of excellence One focused on global geospatial knowledge, another focused on geodesy, and a third, soon to open, focused on the future geospatial ecosystems. And so I think that's a great example of how recommendations have been put into action. Thank you.

I thank you and I thank all panelists for their valuable insight. I now will proceed to the closing remarks on behalf of Ambassador Benjamin, Vice President in Charge for the Management Segment. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, my appreciation again to all for the commitment and expertise you have brought our discussion. Your insights come at a pivotal moment. Today's global challenges demand greater responsiveness, which requires stronger coherence and coordination. We have heard about the value of bringing together data, knowledge, and policy approaches to address the complex and interrelated challenges of sustainable development. We have also heard about the importance of effective monitoring, follow-up, and accountability mechanisms in helping intergovernmental commitments into tangible actions towards achieving the SDGs. A recurring theme throughout our exchanges has been the importance of fostering stronger connections between the ECOSOC subsidiary bodies and to build on their mandates, institutions, and areas of expertise to ensure better support to Member States in advancing integrated solutions that can yield more effective and lasting results. Dear colleagues, the challenge before us is to ensure that this ecosystem operates not as a collection of individual bodies, but as a mutually reinforcing system that harnesses its collective expertise to generate greater impact in support of the Sustainable Development Goals. Today's discussion will help inform ongoing review process and future efforts to strengthen the effectiveness of the Council and its subsidiary machinery, in particular ECOSOC's upcoming review of its subsidiary bodies. I look forward to working with you all to ensure a meaningful and impactful review. I thank you. I briefly pause the meeting to rearrange the podium. Please remain seated. I invite the Council to begin its consideration of Agenda Item 12, Coordination, Programme and Adequations, Reports of Coordination Bodies, to hold a dialogue with the Secretariat of the United Nations System, Chief Executive Board for Coordination. Ms. Maike Jansen, to introduce the Annual Overview Report of the United Nations System Chief Executives Board for Coordination for 2025, as contained in Document E/2026/50. Ms. Jansen, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. Vice President. Thank you, distinguished delegates. The Council has before it the Annual Overview Report of the United Nations System Chief Executives Board for Coordination, CEB, for 2025, describing major activities carried out under the Board's auspices. Over the course of 2025, the Board continued to advance coherence across the United Nations system in support of Member States and implementation of intergovernmental mandates. Against the backdrop of complex and interconnected global challenges, Board members emphasized the importance of multilateral cooperation and collective action in delivering coordinated and effective responses. As you will see in the reports, through the High-Level Committee on Programs, HLCP, organizations advance work on key policy issues requiring system-wide engagement, including demographic change, transnational organized crime, artificial intelligence, measures of progress beyond GDP, and climate action. These efforts generated practical outcomes, including common messages, policy dialogues, and coordinated approaches, thereby strengthening policy coherence and support to Member States. The Committee also continued to support implementation of the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries and preparations towards its midterm review. Through CEB's High-Level Committee on Management, HLCM, organizations prioritized efforts to strengthen resilience and impacts— and the impact of United Nations operations. In the context of sustained financial constraints, coordinated action was undertaken to safeguard mandate delivery and operational integrity. Work focused on advancing a portfolio of far-reaching efficiency initiatives, to simplify, integrate, and modernize core business operations, as well as on strengthening risk management, enhancing digital solutions, expanding system-wide statistics, and promoting data-driven decision-making to support transparency and accountability. The Board also continued to advance priorities including disability inclusion, multilingualism, and efforts to prevent and address sexual harassment. These initiatives contribute to a more inclusive, effective, and accountable organization. The experiences reflected in the annual overview reports are relevant in the context of reform efforts in the UN, including the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative. They demonstrate how CEB and its mechanisms are supporting efforts to enhance effectiveness and efficiency by fostering coherence, and leveraging the comparative advantages of organizations across the system, while remaining firmly grounded in the mandates that have been established by Member States. System-wide coordination is ever more essential in delivering intergovernmental mandates. In today's demanding environments, the logic is simple: when the system aligns, it delivers more, and when it delivers together, it delivers better. Because coordination is not an added layer, it is a force multiplier and an enabler. So I trust this report demonstrates how CEB continues to serve as a platform for coherence, coordination, and collective problem-solving across the UN system, in support of Member States and the people it serves. I welcome the Council's view on the work of the Board, and I thank you very much.
